title: Reliable machine-checked mathematical discovery

concept.text: The innovation is a system that repeatedly discovers new research mathematics and produces proofs that a standard proof assistant can check. Across a demanding portfolio of previously open statements, it would find the mathematical argument without humans supplying it, then deliver a kernel-checked proof or formally verified disproof, together with explanations and mathematical libraries that other researchers can inspect, maintain and extend. This describes a target capability, not a promise to resolve every open statement.

Discovery and verification perform different jobs. The discovery system must find useful definitions, intermediate results and arguments; the proof assistant checks whether the resulting formal proof establishes the precisely encoded statement under its declared axioms. People must still assess whether that statement faithfully captures the intended mathematical question. AlphaProof’s research identifies a further transition from solving isolated problems to building theories by expanding the library with new concepts.

Olympiad solutions, convincing natural-language arguments and formalizations of theorems already proved by humans supply important components of this capability. None alone demonstrates repeatable autonomous discovery at research depth. Similarly, a company announcement can report a substantial advance without establishing independent reproduction, broad repeatability or community-ready libraries. The supplied evidence does not establish whether the complete target capability remains absent as of 1 November 2026.

significance.text: Reliable discovery coupled to formal verification would provide a new way to produce mathematical knowledge: a machine could contribute an original research result accompanied by an argument whose formal validity can be checked mechanically. This conditional impact goes beyond producing plausible prose or translating an existing human proof. Lean’s checking provides a strong technical basis for confidence, relative to the declared axioms and the soundness of its kernel; it does not automatically establish novelty, faithful problem formulation or community acceptance.

Long machine-generated arguments make this separation especially valuable because their apparent plausibility can exceed a reader’s ability to inspect every step. New Scientist reports IMO organizer Joseph Myers arguing that formal proofs are central to confidence in lengthy AI solutions. Human-readable explanations and reusable libraries would add a different benefit: enabling mathematicians to understand the ideas, build on intermediate results and integrate the work into subsequent research.

Conditional synthesis: a dependable supply of new theorems and reusable theories could accelerate research in mathematics and, where those results are relevant, theoretical computer science or other sciences. Such downstream transformation would depend on the importance of the discoveries and their successful adoption. Formal mathematical correctness alone does not validate an empirical model, establish engineering usefulness or guarantee that the system chooses worthwhile questions.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central challenge is to combine original research reasoning, dependable formalization and reusable theory development in a repeatable autonomous process. AlphaProof demonstrates substantial formal problem solving, but its authors distinguish that achievement from research-level theory building, which requires introducing concepts and continuously extending mathematical libraries. Its reliance on expert formalization of competition statements also illustrates why finding a proof after receiving a formal problem is a narrower achievement than carrying an informal research question through to a faithful formal result.

Engineering synthesis: a convincing system must manage long chains of dependent lemmas, select productive abstractions, recover from failed approaches and keep proof search within practical computational limits. It must distinguish proving the intended statement from proving an easier mistranslation, expose its axiom dependencies and identify when a proposed counterexample actually disproves the original claim. These requirements concern the whole discovery process; a successful final kernel check addresses only part of them.

A further barrier is converting generated formal material into a maintainable mathematical resource. Anthropic’s Fermat’s Last Theorem report says that its mostly machine-written library was not yet in a form acceptable to Mathlib. Its scale illustrates the integration challenge, but a large line count alone does not establish that a library is unauditable or unusable. Organization, explanations, dependencies and compatibility with community libraries matter alongside size.

Evaluation synthesis: repeatability and autonomy also require evidence beyond a single successful output. A demanding assessment must document human assistance, unsuccessful attempts, computational resources and independent rebuilding across multiple mathematical areas. The supplied record contains important partial achievements and reported research claims, but cannot establish the complete capability’s presence or global absence.

current_state.text: At the 2024 International Mathematical Olympiad, AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry 2 together achieved a silver-equivalent score of 28/42. AlphaProof solved three of the five non-geometry problems, P1, P2 and P6, after experts formalized their statements. Each solved problem used approximately 2–3 days of test-time reinforcement learning. AlphaGeometry 2 solved the geometry problem, P4; the two combinatorics problems, P3 and P5, remained unsolved. These were formal competition-mathematics results with substantial computation and human statement preparation, rather than autonomous discoveries of open research mathematics. The Nature account was published on 12 November 2025.

In July 2025, the supplied reporting describes Gemini Deep Think achieving an officially graded and certified gold-level IMO result, while OpenAI reported comparable performance assessed through blind grading by three former IMO medalists organized by OpenAI. Both accounts describe five solved problems out of six, natural-language proofs and the contest schedule of two 4.5-hour sessions. Five full-credit seven-point solutions imply 35/42; that score is an inference from the reported performance. Neither retained report establishes which problem was missed, so the earlier identification of Problem 6 is not retained.

On 4 September 2026, Anthropic announced a largely autonomous Lean formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem completed in 11 days, reporting approximately 13 million lines of Lean and 29,500 intermediate theorems. The effort followed an existing exposition of Wiles’s proof, so its central achievement was formalizing a known theorem. The accompanying report describes rebuilding all 29,511 project cards from source outside the working platform, a single-project build, restrictions to standard axioms, statement comparison using comparator, Lean kernel replay and nanoda checks. The card count and intermediate-theorem count describe different reported quantities. These checks strengthen the reported verification basis, but the supplied review did not independently reproduce the build, and using separate checking software is not equivalent to reproduction by an unaffiliated group.

On 8 September 2026, OpenAI announced analytical and Lean-formalized proofs resolving Navier–Stokes alternatives C and D through a singularity construction with smooth external forcing. The retained paper excerpt describes zero initial velocity, a smooth force compactly supported in space and time, and the announcement reports finite energy throughout the dynamics. The official problem formulation retained in the supplied review permits smooth forcing in the breakdown alternatives C and D; forcing therefore does not itself place the claimed result outside the prize formulation. The claim’s scope should nevertheless remain explicit rather than being generalized to every version of the fluid equations.

The supplied review could assess the OpenAI announcement and theorem statement, but not the complete claimed resolution. The retained paper extraction stops in section 5 although its contents extend to page 165; figures were not inspected and Lean files were not supplied for replay. Consequently, this record preserves the announced result without independently certifying its mathematical correctness. Those evidence limitations do not establish that the result is false.

Clay Mathematics Institute’s notice of 11 September 2026 describes the Navier–Stokes problem as apparently settled while explaining that evaluation would proceed slowly; it does not award a prize. The retained MathWorld page, read on 1 November 2026, reports that Clay continued to label the problem Active. The provisional institutional response and pending prize process are compatible. Neither the absence of an award nor MathWorld’s reported label establishes rejection, controversy or mathematical invalidity.

Evidence-scope synthesis: these dated results establish substantial formal reasoning achievements and reports of larger mathematical advances, with the qualifications above. They do not establish the complete repeatable discovery capability proposed here. The supplied freshness-search record is empty, so coverage through 1 November 2026 is not comprehensive; that limitation does not invalidate the supported historical results.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: settle at least three statements documented as open in the peer-reviewed literature when the attempt begins, drawn from different mathematical areas. For each, provide a machine-produced proof or formally verified disproof accepted by a standard proof assistant. Three is a proposed threshold, not an established standard. Such a finite portfolio would demonstrate breadth and repeatability within its tested scope, rather than literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Proof-assistant-accepted machine settlements of three open statements across areas

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirements: record human interventions sufficiently to establish that humans did not supply the argument; release the formal statements, proof sources, dependencies and build instructions; and have a group unaffiliated with the creators independently rebuild each result. Reviewers should inspect statement fidelity and axiom dependencies as well as successful compilation. Report elapsed time, computation and unsuccessful attempts so practical repeatability can be assessed.
completion_criteria.label: Each unaffiliated rebuild shows no human-supplied argument and repeatability records

completion_criteria.text: Proposed usability requirements: accompany the formal artifacts with explanations that specialists can follow and assess whether the generated library can be maintained, reused and extended. Evaluate these properties directly rather than imposing an arbitrary line-count ceiling. One successful but contested solution would not establish repeatability, while a large proof library should be judged by its organization and usefulness rather than its size alone.
completion_criteria.label: Specialist-followable explanations and assessed library maintenance, reuse and extension

completion_criteria.text: Proposed acceptance requirement: obtain specialist-journal acceptance or, for a relevant Millennium Prize problem, complete the applicable Clay evaluation process. This adds community scrutiny to technical proof checking; the two are separate milestones. The retained Clay rules require at least two years of examination by the global mathematics community. The supplied review treated that rules capture as partial because of extraction issues, while finding the relevant provision readable. A pending prize process should therefore be reported separately from the result’s formal verification.
completion_criteria.label: Specialist-journal acceptance or completed two-year Clay evaluation

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: CSC-03, Competent general machine intelligence, overlaps through reasoning, planning and learning. CSC-07 adds a specific outcome requirement: original research mathematics with formally checked arguments and reusable artifacts. General competence alone does not guarantee those properties, and mathematical discovery alone would not demonstrate general intelligence. This comparison is limited to the supplied roster title because a full definition of CSC-03 was not provided.

Roster-based synthesis: CSC-04, Industrial-cost proof-carrying software, and CSC-10, Machine-checked behavioral guarantees for frontier learned models, share an emphasis on formally checkable evidence. Their stated targets concern software and learned-model behavior, respectively; CSC-07 concerns discovering mathematical results. Improvements in automated proof construction could assist all three, but success in one would not automatically satisfy the others’ scope or practical requirements.

Roster-based synthesis: CSC-01, Practical polynomial-time algorithms for NP-complete problems, and CSC-06, A predictive theory of generalization for modern learning systems, describe particular algorithmic or theoretical breakthroughs that could become subjects of mathematical discovery. CSC-07 is a capability for producing results across a research portfolio. Demonstrating it would not by itself establish either of those specific breakthroughs.

Roster-based synthesis: CSC-02, Application-scale fault-tolerant quantum computation; CSC-05, Routine-cost general computation on encrypted data; and CSC-09, Practical indistinguishability obfuscation, involve computational capabilities whose mathematical foundations could benefit from better automated discovery. Their practical resource, implementation and security requirements remain separate from producing checked theorems. CSC-08, General-purpose physical autonomy in unmodified environments, could also benefit from improved reasoning, but additionally requires effective perception and action in the physical world, beyond CSC-07’s mathematical scope.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish whether the complete target capability is present or absent as of 1 November 2026; the freshness-search record is empty.
The complete OpenAI Navier–Stokes argument and Lean proof were not validated in the supplied review. Independent correctness, reproduction and the eventual Clay evaluation remain unresolved here.
The supplied record does not establish unaffiliated reproduction of Anthropic’s Fermat’s Last Theorem formalization or its eventual readiness for community-library integration.
The identity of the problem missed by each reported 2025 IMO system is not established by the retained reports.
Practical resource limits, acceptable human assistance and maintainability benchmarks for a repeatable discovery system still require explicit evaluation choices.
Detailed definitions of the other roster concepts were not supplied. The review’s caution about CSC-03 is retained through a qualified title-level comparison rather than complete omission.

brief.title: New mathematics with proofs computers can check
possible: Mathematicians could ask a machine to tackle an open question and receive a new proof—or a disproof—that a proof assistant, software that checks mathematical arguments, accepts. The machine would find the argument without a person supplying it.

Researchers could follow explanations of the ideas and build on libraries, reusable collections of mathematical definitions and proofs. The system would keep producing results across different mathematical fields.
why: This would give mathematicians a dependable way to gain new knowledge with proofs that software can check step by step. That checking would be especially valuable for arguments too long for a reader to inspect closely.

Understandable explanations and reusable proofs would help researchers extend the discoveries. Useful results could also accelerate theoretical computer science and other sciences that depend on mathematics.

sources.showed: Their systems reached gold-level performance in an international mathematics competition using written proofs. Google's result received official grading; OpenAI arranged separate grading.
sources.quote: Experimental AI models from Google DeepMind and OpenAI have achieved a gold-level performance in the International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO) for the first time.
sources.cited_for: Competition results demonstrate progress in mathematical reasoning.
sources.not_established: Competition solutions do not establish repeated discovery of new research mathematics with computer-checked proofs.

sources.showed: AlphaProof solved difficult competition problems using Lean proof-checking software. Experts translated the questions into computer-readable statements, and solutions required days of computation.
sources.quote: AlphaProof substantially improves state-of-the-art results on historical mathematics competition problems.
sources.cited_for: Machines can find difficult mathematical arguments that proof-checking software accepts.
sources.not_established: This does not demonstrate autonomous discovery of open research results or sustained development of new mathematical theories.

sources.showed: Anthropic reports that Claude largely autonomously converted an existing proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem into Lean. Its generated library was not yet suitable for Mathlib, a shared mathematical library.
sources.quote:
Claude ran largely autonomously
for eleven days before completing the proof.
sources.cited_for: A machine can undertake a large conversion of known mathematics into computer-checkable proofs.
sources.not_established: Formalizing a known proof does not establish original discovery, independent reproduction or a library ready for community use.

sources.quote: Our system produced an analytical proof and a Lean formalization that an initially smooth fluid at rest can develop a singularity in a finite time.
sources.cited_for: The announcement reports machine-produced research mathematics accompanied by a computer-checkable proof.
sources.not_established: The claim does not establish independent reproduction, completed community evaluation or repeatable discovery across mathematical fields.

sources.showed: Clay described the fluid-equation problem as apparently settled and said its evaluation process would proceed slowly.
sources.cited_for: Community evaluation remains a separate step after a solution is announced.
sources.not_established: The notice does not establish completed evaluation or award a prize.

sources.showed: Weisstein reports that Clay continued to label the fluid-equation problem Active, with prize evaluation still pending.
sources.cited_for: An announced solution and a pending prize process can coexist.
sources.not_established: An Active status does not establish acceptance, rejection or mathematical correctness.

sources.showed: Both companies reported gold-level competition performance using written proofs. Google's result received official certification; OpenAI used former medalists for blind grading.
sources.quote: OpenAI says its model processed problems as plain text and generated natural-language proofs, operating like a standard language model rather than a purpose-built mathematical system.
sources.cited_for: General reasoning systems can solve demanding competition problems in ordinary mathematical language.
sources.not_established: Written competition proofs do not establish computer-checked discovery of previously open research mathematics.

shown: OpenAI reports a machine-produced solution to a major question about fluid equations, accompanied by a Lean proof. The claim concerns an applied force that varies smoothly. Clay described the problem as apparently settled, with evaluation pending.

Anthropic reports largely autonomous computer-checking of an existing proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem. AlphaProof has produced checked competition proofs. These achievements cover parts of the proposed capability; repeated autonomous research discovery remains to be demonstrated.
missing: Repeated autonomous discovery across mathematical fields still needs to be demonstrated.
Independent teams need to rebuild the proofs and confirm that the encoded questions match the intended mathematics.
Generated libraries need to demonstrate that researchers can understand, maintain and extend them.

milestones.label: Checked settlements of three open questions across mathematical fields
milestones.explanation: A machine would settle at least three questions from different fields, documented as open in peer-reviewed literature when work begins, with software-accepted proofs or disproofs. This would demonstrate breadth and repetition.

milestones.label: Independent rebuilds establish autonomy and repeatability
milestones.explanation: Unaffiliated teams would rebuild released proofs, check statements and assumptions, and examine logs of human help, failures, time and computing. This would establish that humans supplied no argument and test repeatability.

milestones.label: Specialists can understand, maintain and extend the mathematics
milestones.explanation: Specialists would follow the explanations and assess whether the libraries can be maintained, reused and extended. This would establish their usefulness for further research.

milestones.label: Journal acceptance or completed Clay evaluation
milestones.explanation: Results would gain specialist-journal acceptance or complete the applicable Clay evaluation, including at least two years of community examination. This would add community scrutiny to software checking.

uncertain: The fluid-equation claim still awaits independent reproduction and completed community evaluation.
Acceptable human assistance, computing costs and library-maintenance standards remain open evaluation choices.
The proposed breadth threshold is a judgment about repeatability, rather than an established scientific standard.

page.title: Autonomous mathematical discovery with formal proofs
page.definition: An AI system repeatedly settles open research questions in different mathematical fields without human-supplied arguments. It supplies proofs checked by a proof assistant, software that verifies formal deductions from declared axioms, and creates reusable definitions and lemmas.

goal.need: Anthropic’s Fermat formalization illustrates the scale of checking an existing argument. In its 2024 IMO evaluation, AlphaProof solved 3 of 5 non-geometry problems, requiring 2–3 days per solved problem. The goal is to extend machine-checked proof search to new research arguments and reusable mathematical definitions.

figures.note: These are company-reported quantities, not peer-reviewed results. The formalization follows an existing exposition of the proof.

statements.quote: developing an AI co-author capable of proposing and proving useful abstractions.
statements.context: The stated goal of the Exponentiating Mathematics programme.

statements.quote: moving beyond pure problem solving to theory building—the continuous expansion of this library with new concepts.
statements.context: The authors describe the transition from competition problems to research mathematics; the library is Mathlib.

statements.quote: Formalization is also a major factor in how humans can gain confidence in AI-generated mathematical results.

completion.title: The same system repeatedly discovers new research mathematics with checked proofs and reusable theory.
completion.criterion: The same system settles distinct previously open research questions in different mathematical areas without humans supplying the arguments. Specialists confirm novelty and that each formal statement captures the intended question. Released proofs or disproofs pass a proof assistant’s kernel under its declared standard axioms. The system also supplies explanations and new definitions and lemmas accepted for reuse through a community mathematical library’s review process.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; no external combined completion criterion located.
completion.basis: Searched DARPA expMath’s programme and solicitation, Formal Conjectures’ evaluation rules, Lean’s validation guidance and Mathlib’s contribution rules. None defines a combined completion test for repeatable autonomous research discovery and reusable theory. This Atlas synthesis joins their component tests without specifying an unsupported portfolio size or success rate. The cited results do not establish the combined test.

milestones.title: An AI-generated mathematical proof passes Lean’s kernel using only standard axioms.
milestones.criterion: A machine-generated proof is accepted by Lean’s kernel for the intended formal statement, using only its standard foundational axioms and no unproved placeholders. The statement and its referenced definitions must express the intended mathematics. In the 2024 IMO evaluation, AlphaProof supplied Lean proofs for problems P1, P2 and P6 after experts formalized the statements.
milestones.set_by: Lean developers, The Lean Language Reference, Validating a Lean Proof; this criterion applies to the Lean route.
milestones.threshold_quote: the Lean kernel has accepted a proof of that theorem statement

milestones.title: An AI formalizes a known research proof in Lean using only its three standard axioms.
milestones.criterion: The system converts an existing research argument into a Lean 4 proof. Formal Conjectures requires kernel acceptance using at most propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound, excluding unproved placeholders and native-evaluation axioms. The informal argument may be supplied. Anthropic reported this kind of result for Fermat’s Last Theorem on 4 September 2026, following an existing exposition; the company report is not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: Formal Conjectures authors, Evaluation Framework: Proof Auto-formalization and Correctness.
milestones.threshold_quote: accepted by the kernel using at most the standard Lean 4 axioms

milestones.title: An AI settles an open research conjecture with a checked proof and confirmed statement fidelity.
milestones.criterion: An AI supplies the first proof or disproof of an open research conjecture, accepted by Lean under the benchmark’s allowed axioms; manual inspection confirms statement fidelity. The AlphaProof Nexus author preprint, revised on 8 June 2026, reports 9 successes from 353 Erdős problems and 44 from 492 OEIS conjectures. OpenAI announced a Lean-formalized, smoothly forced Navier–Stokes singularity on 8 September 2026; that announcement is not peer reviewed. Clay’s notice of 11 September 2026 leaves evaluation pending.
milestones.set_by: Formal Conjectures authors, Evaluation Framework: New Formal Proof Discovery and Evaluating Open Problems.
milestones.threshold_quote: the first kernel-accepted proof provides an uncontaminated success signal

milestones.title: Mathlib maintainers merge definitions and lemmas produced by the system’s research proof search.
milestones.criterion: Definitions and lemmas generated during the system’s research proof search pass Mathlib review and are merged by its maintainers. Review covers generality, integration, maintainability, documentation and a usable interface for subsequent proofs. A human contributor must understand the AI-generated material and justify its design decisions. Anthropic’s Fermat repository describes itself as a research artifact that is not maintained and does not accept contributions; that release does not establish Mathlib acceptance.
milestones.set_by: Mathlib maintainers, Contributing to mathlib and Pull Request Review Guide; this criterion is specific to the Lean/Mathlib route.
milestones.threshold_quote: Mathlib intentionally has very high standards (on generality, integration with the remaining library and maintainability, including code style).

not_found: No primary report was located establishing Mathlib acceptance of Anthropic’s generated Fermat library.
The AlphaProof Nexus journal page could not be opened; its full author preprint was accessible.
